description: USDA soil texture classes with the hydraulic and erosion properties the water balance and RUSLE modules need. Class centroids are PRIORS for when only a texture name is known; whenever measured sand/silt/clay fractions or local soil survey values are available they must override these.

units.sand_pct / silt_pct / clay_pct: percent by mass of the mineral fraction (<2mm), class centroid
units.theta_sat / theta_fc / theta_wp: volumetric water content m3/m3 at saturation, field capacity (-33 kPa) and permanent wilting point (-1500 kPa)
units.rew_mm: FAO-56 readily evaporable water: depth evaporable from the surface layer at the maximum rate before stage-2 drying begins
units.hydrologic_group: NRCS hydrologic soil group A-D, used for the SCS curve-number runoff term

provenance: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 (Allen et al., 1998) Table 19 - theta_fc, theta_wp and REW ranges by texture class
Rawls, Brakensiek & Saxton (1982) - saturated hydraulic conductivity and porosity by texture
Saxton & Rawls (2006) - water characteristic estimates from texture
USDA NRCS National Engineering Handbook Part 630 - hydrologic soil group assignment and curve numbers
USDA soil texture triangle (NRCS) - classification boundaries
known_gaps: These are class centroids. Within-class variation in theta_fc is wide (FAO-56 Table 19 quotes ranges, not points), so total available water from a texture NAME alone can be off by 30-40 percent. Measured fractions should always win.

Organic matter raises water holding capacity and lowers erodibility, and is not in this table - it enters through the RothC carbon state instead, which is the point: the simulator must let improving SOC feed back into water holding, not treat soil as static.
Stone content, hardpans, sodicity and shrink-swell cracking are all absent. Vertisols in particular crack and bypass-flow in ways a single-layer bucket model cannot represent.
Hydrologic group ignores depth to restrictive layer and water table, which NRCS uses alongside texture. A shallow soil over rock behaves like group D regardless of its texture.
theta_sat here is total porosity; effective saturation in the field is typically 85-95 percent of it because of entrapped air.

textures.name: Sand
textures.notes: Very low water holding capacity: a crop here depends on rainfall frequency, not seasonal total, and a deep-rooted crop buys little because there is little water to reach. Drains too fast to waterlog but leaches nitrate readily.

textures.name: Loamy sand
textures.notes: Still droughty. Cover crop residue has a disproportionate effect here because surface mulch cuts the high soil evaporation these soils suffer.

textures.name: Sandy loam
textures.notes: Workable and well drained with moderate storage. Among the most erodible textures once bare, because particles detach easily and there is little clay to bind aggregates.

textures.name: Loam
textures.notes: The agronomic reference texture: good storage, good drainage, wide crop choice. Rotation changes show up here as yield and margin effects rather than as hard feasibility constraints.

textures.name: Silt loam
textures.notes: High available water, but silt-dominated surfaces crust and seal under raindrop impact, so infiltration collapses mid-storm and runoff rises even on gentle slopes. One of the textures where keeping the surface covered matters most.

textures.name: Silt
textures.notes: Rare as a field texture. Highly erodible: almost no clay to stabilise aggregates and particles in the size range most easily detached and transported.

textures.name: Sandy clay loam
textures.notes: Enough clay to hold water and resist detachment, enough sand to stay workable. Prone to compaction and subsurface hardpans under machinery, which is where a deep-rooted crop such as pigeonpea earns its place.

textures.name: Clay loam
textures.notes: Good storage but slow intake, so high-intensity rainfall runs off rather than infiltrating. Narrow workable moisture window: sticky when wet, hard when dry, which is a real equipment and timing constraint for a farmer, not just a model parameter.

textures.name: Silty clay loam
textures.notes: High available water with poor intake. Combines silt crusting with clay's slow conductivity, so it both seals and drains slowly - waterlogging risk is real for sensitive crops.

textures.name: Sandy clay
textures.notes: Uncommon. Clay-dominated behaviour with sand's low fertility retention.

textures.name: Silty clay
textures.notes: Very slow intake and poor aeration. Rooting is often restricted by physical impedance well before water or nutrients become limiting.

textures.name: Clay
textures.notes: Large total water store but a modest usable fraction, because much is held below wilting point. High clay also slows organic matter turnover, which RothC represents through the clay-dependent CO2 partition - so high-clay soils gain carbon more readily from the same residue input. Shrink-swell cracking creates bypass flow a single-layer bucket model cannot capture; flag this where Vertisols dominate.
